questions.question: In CMOS digital circuit design, why is a transmission gate (pass gate) constructed using a complementary pair of parallel nMOS and pMOS transistors rather than a single nMOS transistor?
options: An nMOS transistor cannot pass a logic '1' without a threshold voltage drop (VDD - Vth), so the parallel pMOS is required to pull the output rail-to-rail to full VDD.
A single nMOS transistor exhibits excessive reverse-bias body effect that permanently latches the output node into a high-impedance state.
The pMOS transistor is necessary solely to reduce the gate input capacitance, thereby doubling the maximum switching frequency of the transmission gate.
An nMOS pass transistor suffers from punch-through breakdown whenever transmitting a logic '0', requiring the pMOS to shunt the ground current.
The complementary pair is required to create a positive-feedback bistable latch that actively drives capacitive loads without static power dissipation.

questions.question: In Network-on-Chip (NoC) architectures employing wormhole routing for multi-core processors, what is the primary architectural purpose of implementing Virtual Channels (VCs)?
options: To encrypt packet payloads at the router crossbar to ensure secure inter-core memory isolation.
To prevent routing deadlocks and mitigate head-of-line blocking by multiplexing multiple independent packet queues over a single physical link.
To dynamically alter the clock frequency of the network router based on instantaneous network packet traffic density.
To eliminate the need for physical buffer memory within the input and output ports of the on-chip routers.
To allow packets to travel concurrently in opposite physical directions over the exact same metal wires using time-division multiplexing.

questions.question: In superscalar processor microarchitecture, which type of data dependency represents a 'true dependency' that cannot be eliminated through register renaming, inherently dictating the flow of computation?
options: Write-After-Write (WAW) / Output dependency
Write-After-Read (WAR) / Anti-dependency
Read-After-Write (RAW) / Flow dependency
Read-After-Read (RAR) / Input dependency
Control-After-Write (CAW) / Speculative dependency

questions.question: In multi-supply voltage (Multi-VDD) digital IC design, why is an up-level shifter strictly required when a signal travels from a lower-voltage domain (VDDL) to a higher-voltage domain (VDDH)?
options: The lower-voltage signal lacks sufficient charge to overcome the electromigration threshold of the receiving domain's interconnects.
The difference in operating voltages causes the receiving gate to undergo spontaneous dielectric gate-oxide breakdown under normal bias.
The logic thresholds of standard CMOS gates scale with clock frequency, causing total clock phase inversion between different voltage islands.
If VDDL directly drives a VDDH-powered gate, the input voltage cannot completely turn off the receiving pMOS transistor, resulting in excessive static crowbar current.
Signals driven at VDDL travel faster than signals at VDDH, inevitably causing widespread hold-time violations at the domain interface.

questions.question: In scan-based Design for Testability (DFT) for digital ASICs, what is the principal implementation challenge of Launch-on-Shift (LOS) at-speed delay testing compared to Launch-on-Capture (LOC) testing?
options: LOS requires replacing all edge-triggered flip-flops with dual-edge-triggered master-slave registers, doubling silicon area.
LOS cannot detect transition delay faults on combinational paths with high logical depth, limiting fault coverage to under 50%.
LOS mandates that all on-chip clock domains operate asynchronously during test mode, causing unavoidable metastability across scan chains.
LOS requires generating test patterns using sequential Automatic Test Pattern Generation (ATPG), which has intractable exponential runtime complexity.
LOS requires the scan enable (SE) control signal to transition from shift to capture mode at full functional clock speed, demanding high-speed clock-like routing.
